Every node ends with exactly the degree in its pill." width="100%"} Creates a new graph where each node has the specified degree. Stubs are created for each node (one per degree unit) and then randomly paired. The resulting graph may contain self-loops and multi-edges. Because every stub is used exactly once, each node ends up with exactly the requested degree (a self-loop counts twice toward its node's degree). Apart from that constraint the wiring is completely random, which makes this the standard null model for asking whether a network property is explained by its degree distribution alone: - comparing clustering, path lengths, or assortativity of an observed network against random graphs with the same degrees - testing whether motifs or communities are more frequent than degrees alone predict - generating synthetic networks with a heavy-tailed or otherwise prescribed degree distribution This method doesn't use or modify the graph it is called on (other than recording the step); it builds and returns an entirely new `Graph`, so it can be called on an empty `ec.Graph()`. Nodes are labelled `"0"`, `"1"`, ... in the order of `degree_sequence=`. Self-loops and multi-edges become rare as the graph grows, but with small or very uneven sequences they are common; chain `simplify()` on the result to remove them, at the cost of slightly lowering the affected degrees. For a null model that keeps the graph simple, see `degree_preserving_rewire()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [degree_sequence]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of non-negative integers specifying the degree of each node, one entry per node (entry `i` belongs to the node labelled `str(i)`). For undirected graphs the sum must be even, since every edge uses two stubs. An empty list gives an empty graph. [directed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, generates a directed graph where each entry is used as both the out-degree and the in-degree of its node: out-stubs and in-stubs are shuffled separately and paired, so the sum does not have to be even. If `False` (default), generates an undirected graph. The directedness of the graph the method is called on is ignored. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same `degree_sequence=` always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the result differs on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with the specified degree sequence. The original graph is unchanged. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the degree sequence contains a negative number, or if `directed=` is `False` and the sequence has an odd sum. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node gets exactly the degree asked for. Node labels are the positions in the sequence, so `"0"` has degree `3`, `"1"`, `"2"`, and `"3"` have degree `2`, and `"4"` has degree `1`: ::: {#d0b77afa .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().configuration_model([3, 2, 2, 2, 1], seed=2) { graph.get_label_from_id(nid): graph.get_degree(nid) for nid in sorted(graph.get_node_ids()) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'0': 3, '1': 2, '2': 2, '3': 2, '4': 1} ``` ::: ::: Random stub pairing can produce multi-edges: here `"0"` and `"2"` are joined twice, so the graph is not simple: ::: {#433910f1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True), graph.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (['1--3', '0--1', '3--4', '0--2', '0--2'], False) ``` ::: ::: Chaining `simplify()` removes the duplicate edge, but then node `"0"` and node `"2"` each lose a unit of degree: ::: {#a5b4923c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.simplify().get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['1--3', '0--1', '3--4', '0--2'] ``` ::: ::: A typical use is building a null model for an observed network. Ten disjoint six-node cliques have perfect clustering; a configuration model with the same degrees (every node has degree `5`) has the same number of edges but almost no clustering, showing that the clustering comes from the structure and not from the degrees: ::: {#f43d6ef3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} observed = ec.Graph() for _ in range(10): observed.add_full_graph(n=6) degrees = [observed.get_degree(nid) for nid in observed.get_node_creation_order()] null = ec.Graph().configuration_model(degrees, seed=23) ( (observed.count_edges(), round(observed.average_clustering_coefficient(), 3)), (null.count_edges(), round(null.average_clustering_coefficient(), 3)), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ((150, 1.0), (150, 0.068)) ``` ::: ::: With `directed=True`, each entry becomes both the in-degree and the out-degree of its node, shown here as `(in, out)` pairs: ::: {#3eb0e2e0 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ec.Graph().configuration_model([2, 1, 1, 0], directed=True, seed=4) { directed.get_label_from_id(nid): ( directed.get_in_degree(nid), directed.get_out_degree(nid) ) for nid in sorted(directed.get_node_ids()) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` {'0': (2, 2), '1': (1, 1), '2': (1, 1), '3': (0, 0)} ``` ::: :::
